content: Carefully selected strategies may be considered in specific circumstances to expand access to treatment rather than leaving patients untreated. For instance, ablation can be an option for a carefully chosen, small type 2 transformation zone where the probe tip can achieve complete ablation of the squamocolumnar junction epithelium. This means the probe must reach the full extent, depth, and upper limit of the transformation zone. Adequate training for the selection of cases and follow-up care is essential in such scenarios. Persistent, residual, or recurrent disease is defined as the detection of a histopathologically verified high-grade lesion, including high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL) as per the Lower Anogenital Squamous Terminology (LAST) system. This includes HSIL-CIN 2, HSIL-CIN 3, high-grade CIN (CIN 2 and CIN 3), HSIL not otherwise specified, and adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS). These diagnoses are made from punch biopsies or subsequent surgical specimens, such as hysterectomy, cold knife conization (CKC), or large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ), at any time after the initial treatment, provided there is no documented absence of disease in the interim. Persistent or residual disease excludes cancers confirmed after diagnosis with surgical specimens. Recurrent disease is defined as the detection of a high-grade lesion following a documented absence of such lesions after initial treatment. Studies often use the terms persistent/residual disease and recurrence interchangeably without distinguishing between them. However, both conditions represent treatment failures. Some studies use terms like cure or treatment success to indicate the absence of persistent, residual, or recurrent disease following initial treatment and estimate rates accordingly. The specific location of the lesion on the cervix detected during follow-up is not critical, as the goal of cervical pre-cancer treatment is to address the entire transformation zone rather than a specific lesion. Any lesion detected during follow-up should be considered a treatment failure, with the final diagnosis based on the worst histopathological outcome. Symptoms of persistent or recurrent disease are generally non-specific. Consequences include the need for retreatment, adverse psychological impacts, and resource implications such as costs, human resources, and hospital services. Assessment methods vary across studies, with some using random punch biopsies on all treated women during follow-up, while others rely on negative HPV tests, cytology, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), or normal colposcopy as evidence of disease absence. Sensitivity analyses should be conducted to account for these differences in assessment methods. Treatment of recurrent or persistent HSIL/CIN 2/CIN 3 includes LLETZ or ablation, depending on eligibility and the availability of treatment techniques. AIS is treated with LLETZ or CKC. These treatments can be administered by colposcopists, general practitioners, or nurses. Invasive cancers require radical surgery or radiation therapy in specialized settings, with additional testing for metastasis as needed. The incidence of histopathological high-grade lesions and cancers (HSIL+ or CIN 2+) refers to new cases detected following treatment. This includes histological HSIL (HSIL-CIN 2 and HSIL-CIN 3), high-grade CIN (CIN 2 and CIN 3), HSIL not otherwise specified, AIS, invasive squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and unspecified carcinoma. All categories are combined as HSIL+ or CIN 2+. Symptoms are non-specific, and consequences include the need for treatment of high-grade lesions or invasive cancer, psychological distress, and resource implications. New cases are detected through linkage with screening registries or active follow-up of the screening cohort. Rates of HSIL+ or CIN 2+ can be calculated annually based on the number of women under active surveillance diagnosed with CIN 2/3 in a given year divided by the number screened in that year. Cumulative rates may be expressed as cases per 100,000 person-years of observation. The incidence of cervical cancer includes newly diagnosed cases of invasive cervical cancer (squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, or unspecified invasive cancer) in the population under consideration within a defined time period, typically at least six months after screening and treatment. Symptoms may include vaginal discharge, irregular bleeding, and pain. Consequences include the need for further investigations and treatment, psychological distress, potential disability, and fatality depending on the stage at diagnosis, as well as resource implications. New cases are histopathologically diagnosed through active follow-up or linkage to screening and cancer registries. Incidence is documented as cases per 100,000 person-years of observation. Mortality from cervical cancer refers to deaths reported from cervical cancer in the population under consideration following treatment within a defined time period. This is assessed through linkage with population-based cancer registries and mortality databases or active follow-up. No specific thresholds or treatments are applicable, and the time horizon is any time following treatment. Treatment coverage is defined as the proportion of eligible women treated in a population. It is calculated as the number of women completing treatment within a defined time frame divided by the total number of screen-positive women eligible for treatment during the same period, multiplied by 100. Low treatment coverage increases the risk of invasive cancer and mortality among detected women and reduces the impact of screening programs on cervical cancer incidence and mortality. Data are collected through information systems or screening registries with linkage between screening and treatment services. The same-day treatment rate in a screen-and-treat approach is the proportion of eligible women treated on the same day as screening. This is calculated as the number of women treated on the same day divided by the number of women eligible for same-day treatment, multiplied by 100. Low compliance with same-day treatment increases the risk of invasive cancer and mortality and reduces the effectiveness of screening programs. Data are collected systematically through health information systems. Screening coverage at the population level is the proportion of screening-eligible women undergoing screening within a defined time frame. It is calculated as the number of women screened divided by the total number of screening-eligible women during the same period, multiplied by 100. Low screening coverage increases the risk of invasive cancer and mortality and reduces the impact of screening programs. Data may be collected through information systems, registries, or surveys. Each program has its own cycle for estimating coverage, ranging from one to five years, but annual calculations are preferable.
